common_name: Alba Maxima Rose (Jacobite Rose, Great Double White)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; Alba Maxima is an ancient variety of unrecorded origin, documented in Europe since at least the late 1500s and long associated with the Jacobite cause in Scotland.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Alba Maxima is an ancient variety of unrecorded origin, documented in European herbals since the late 1500s and long associated with the Jacobite cause in Scotland, where it is still called the Jacobite rose. It opens from blush-pink buds into fully double, pure white flowers with faint yellow highlights, set against distinctive blue-gray foliage, blooming in one abundant flush in early summer. This tough, suckering shrub tolerates poor soil, partial shade, and hard winters better than almost any other old rose, needing only an occasional thinning of old canes after bloom.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; grown in the Netherlands since before 1795 under the names La Belle Sultane and Violacea.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Grown in the Netherlands since before 1795 and sold under the names La Belle Sultane and Violacea, this gallica bears nearly single, rich violet-purple to maroon petals surrounding a bright cluster of gold stamens, a striking contrast rare among old roses. It flowers once in early summer in dense clusters on an upright, suckering shrub, and its modest size and tolerance of lean soil make it a good choice for a mixed border or hedge. Remove only dead or crossing wood, since gallicas set next year's buds on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; attributed to French breeder Julien-Alexandre Hardy before 1836, it spreads readily by suckers like other gallicas.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Attributed to French breeder Julien-Alexandre Hardy before 1836, Gloire de France produces quartered, intensely double flowers that open rich pink and fade to a pale blush at the outer petals, carried on lax, arching canes that spread readily by suckers. It blooms once, in a heavy early-summer flush, with the strong classic rose fragrance typical of the gallica class. Because it suckers freely, give it room to naturalize or confine the roots if used in a tight border.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; bred by R.S. Soetemans in Belgium before 1840, it stays more compact than many damasks.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by R.S. Soetemans in Belgium before 1840, Madame Zoetmans is a compact damask bearing very double, blush-white flowers that age to pure white around a small green button eye, with the rich, sweet fragrance the damask class is prized for. It blooms in a single generous flush in early summer on a tidy, well-branched shrub that stays smaller than many damasks. Prune lightly right after flowering, since like other once-blooming damasks it sets its buds on the prior year's wood.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; traces to seed gathered from the poet Omar Khayyam's grave in Nishapur, Iran.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. This damask traces to seed gathered from a rose growing on the grave of the Persian poet Omar Khayyam in Nishapur, brought back to England in the 1880s and grown on until plants were ceremonially set on the grave of his translator Edward FitzGerald at Boulge, Suffolk, in 1893, an episode organized by writer Edward Clodd of the Omar Khayyam Club. It bears clear pink, double, strongly fragrant flowers in a single early-summer flush on a medium, bushy shrub typical of the damask class. Keep soil evenly moist through bloom and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood afterward.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring against a sturdy support; raised by the English amateur Mr. Blair and introduced before 1834.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Raised by the English amateur Mr. Blair and introduced before 1834, Blairii No. 2 is one of the most vigorous climbing Bourbons, producing large, richly fragrant, pale pink flowers that open from deeper pink buds and fade toward the center. It flowers in one spectacular flush in early summer with only scattered repeat bloom later, so train the long canes horizontally along a fence or pillar to encourage flowering laterals the following year. Give it several years to establish before expecting a full flush, since it rewards patience with great size and vigor.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring; bred by Francois Lacharme in France and introduced in 1867.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by the French rose breeder Francois Lacharme and introduced in 1867, Coquette des Alpes carries large, double, white flowers with a carmine-pink flush at the center, with a sweet, strong fragrance on an upright, vigorous Bourbon shrub. Unlike many antique roses it repeats well through the growing season, especially with regular light feeding and deadheading of spent blooms. Watch for blackspot in humid climates and give it good air circulation, as its pale petals show spotting more readily than darker Bourbons.

scientific_name: Rosa x alba 'Madame Legras de Saint Germain'

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in sun or light shade; introduced in France around 1846 with no breeder recorded.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Introduced in France around 1846 by a breeder whose name was not recorded, Madame Legras de Saint-Germain bears very double, quartered flowers that open creamy lemon-white at the center and fade to pure white, carried on tall, nearly thornless canes with the gray-green foliage typical of Alba roses. It flowers once, in a dependable early-summer flush, and tolerates poor soil and partial shade better than most old roses. Prune only lightly after bloom to remove dead or crossing wood, since it sets flower buds on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring; raised by the French breeder Robert and introduced around 1851-1853.

directions: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter to early spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun. Raised by the French breeder Robert and introduced around the early 1850s, Jeanne de Montfort is one of the tallest moss roses, with heavily mossed buds opening into loosely double, clear pink flowers carrying a light, resinous moss fragrance distinct from the sweeter scent of its petals. Its long canes can be left to arch as a large shrub or loosely tied to a post or low fence for extra height, and it occasionally produces a light second flush in autumn. Remove only dead or damaged wood after the main flush, since heavy pruning sacrifices the following year's mossy buds.
